description.value: The study tested whether perceptual evidence accumulation could be observed in BOLD fMRI by slowing decisions with penalties for incorrect responses and separating detection-related boxcar activity from integration-related ramping activity.

spans.text: We assessed whether evidence accumulation could be observed in the BOLD signal during perceptual decision making.

design.value: Participants performed a slow, event-related random dot motion discrimination task and a matched control task while undergoing fMRI; GLM up-ramp and down-ramp regressors were compared between tasks.

spans.text: We used a control condition in which stimuli and responses were similar to the experimental condition, but that did not engage evidence accumulation of the stimuli.
We performed a multiple linear regression that was designed to distinguish two component processes involved in perceptual decision making: detection and integration.

We performed a three-factor repeated measures ANOVA on beta-weights from our GLM analysis, with task type (dots vs. arrows), ramp regressor type (up-ramp vs. down ramp), and participants (modeled as random effects; AFNI’s 3dANOVA3) as our factors (see Methods).

We used only up-ramp and down-ramp regressors in order to minimize collinearity and thereby reliably distinguish ramping activity from boxcar activity.

2.1. Motion discrimination task

task_description.value: Participants judged the net direction of a cloud of randomly moving dots and responded bimanually with a button box.

spans.text: Participants engaged in a visual decision making task in which they judged the net direction (leftward or rightward) of a cloud of randomly moving dots (Fig. 1A), indicating responses bimanually with a button box.
Each trial began with the onset of moving dots, and participants were free to respond at any time.
The experiment presentation code was written in PsychToolbox (Brainard, 1997).

stimuli.value: Random dot kinematograms with a subset of dots moving coherently left or right.

spans.text: A subset of dots moved coherently either to the left or to the right on each trial, whereas the remainder of dots were distractors that jumped randomly from frame to frame.

Subsequently, whole brain, BOLD-weighted echo-planar images were acquired parallel to the anterior commissure-posterior commissure line with a repetition time of 2 s and echo time of 30 milliseconds while participants performed the task.
Scanning was performed on a 3 T Siemens (Munich, Germany) Allegra scanner.

description.value: Functional images were aligned, slice-time corrected, normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute coordinates, resampled, smoothed, and scaled.

spans.text: Functional images were first aligned to correct for head movement during the scan. Slice timing correction was then performed using sine interpolation. Images were subsequently normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute coordinates (the TT_N27 template) and resampled at 3 × 3 x 3 mm3 resolution. A Gaussian smoothing kernel of 4 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) was applied to improve comparison across subjects, and finally, all time series were scaled to have a mean signal value of 100.
We used AFNI (Cox, 1996) to preprocess the fMRI data.

hrf_model.value: convolved with the hemodynamic response function

spans.text: Our fMRI analysis used up-ramp and down-ramp regressors, the length of which were determined by the dot motion viewing time for each trial, convolved with the hemodynamic response function.

model_settings.value: Ten regressors: up-ramp and down-ramp regressors for dots and arrows trials, plus six motion-correction regressors; third-order polynomial baseline detrending on each twenty-minute scanner run.

spans.text: In total, our GLM had ten regressors for each participant: the up-ramp for the experimental motion discrimination (“dots”) trials, the up-ramp for the control condition (“arrows”) trials, the down-ramp for dots trials, the down-ramp for arrows trials, and six standard motion-correction regressors.
